title: Paying tax by instalments? Your last 2026 payment is due December 15
description: The final 2026 income tax instalment is due Tuesday, December 15. Here's who has to pay, how to check your amount and how to avoid CRA interest.
body_html:
If you are self-employed, earn rental income or have a pension or investment income with little tax taken off, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) may expect you to pay your 2026 tax in instalments. The fourth and final instalment for 2026 is due on Tuesday, December 15, 2026, and the CRA currently charges 7% interest, compounded daily, on amounts that are paid late or short.

What is a tax instalment?

An instalment is a partial payment of the current year's income tax, made during the year instead of in one lump sum at tax time. Employees rarely need it, because tax comes off every paycheque.

For most individuals, 2026 instalments are due on March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. If your main income comes from farming or fishing, you have a single due date of December 31 instead, and the CRA sends that reminder in November.

Who has to pay

For 2026, you have to pay by instalments if both of these are true:

  • your net tax owing for 2026 (roughly, the tax left to pay when you file, after tax already withheld) is more than $3,000 ($1,800 if you live in Quebec on December 31), and
  • your net tax owing was also more than that amount in either 2025 or 2024.

The CRA sends instalment reminders to people it expects will need to pay. The February reminder covers the March and June payments, and the August reminder covers September and December.

A reminder is not a bill. If you are confident your 2026 net tax owing will be $3,000 or less, the CRA says you don't have to pay 2026 instalments, even if you received a reminder. The catch is that if your estimate turns out to be wrong, you may owe interest.

Three ways to work out your amount

The CRA offers three options:

  • No-calculation option: pay the amounts printed on your CRA reminders. These are based on your most recent assessed return. The CRA says this suits people whose income, deductions and credits stay about the same each year.
  • Prior-year option: base your payments on your 2025 return, using the CRA's 2026 instalment calculation chart. This can work well if 2026 looks like 2025 but 2024 was quite different.
  • Current-year option: estimate your actual 2026 tax, CPP contributions and any voluntary EI premiums, and pay based on that. This helps if your income dropped this year, but if your estimate is too low you can be charged interest.

If you choose the prior-year or current-year option and pay the full amounts by each due date, the CRA will not charge instalment interest or a penalty, unless your estimated amounts were too low.

What happens if you pay late or too little

Instalment interest is charged at the CRA's prescribed rate and compounded daily. For October 1 to December 31, 2026, that rate is 7%. You are only charged if the interest for the year is more than $25.

A separate penalty applies only if your instalment interest for 2026 is more than $1,000. In that case, the penalty is half of the amount by which your interest exceeds the greater of $1,000 or 25% of the interest you would have owed if you had made no instalments at all.

There is some good news if you missed or underpaid an earlier 2026 instalment. The CRA says paying your next instalment early, or paying more than required, earns credit interest that can offset the interest on the late or short payment for the same year. This credit can't be refunded or carried to another year.

What to do now

  • Check your August reminder in your CRA account to see the amount the CRA suggests for December.
  • Compare it with your 2026 reality. If your self-employment, rental or investment income changed a lot this year, a quick estimate of your 2026 tax may show you can pay less, or that you should pay more.
  • Pay early enough. The CRA counts the date your payment is received, not the date you sent it. It suggests allowing 3 business days for online payments to show up, and 10 business days for cheques or money orders, before checking that a payment was processed.
  • Use the right account. When paying in person or by mail, use your instalment remittance voucher (form INNS3) so the money goes to your instalment account, not to an older tax debt.
  • Keep proof of payment until it shows in your CRA account or on the instalment summary the CRA sends in February.
  • Think ahead to 2027. If you receive OAS or CPP, you can ask Service Canada to withhold tax from those payments (forms ISP3520OAS and ISP3520CPP), which can reduce or remove the need for instalments.

What it means for small-business owners

If you run a business as a sole proprietor, your business profit is part of your personal return, so these personal instalment rules apply to you. Your instalments also cover CPP contributions on self-employment income. Corporations follow separate instalment rules.

For more on reducing your tax bill as a self-employed person or landlord, see our guides to self-employed expenses and deductions and rental income tax. Our year-end tax checklist covers other steps to take before December 31.

title: Moved from Canada to India this year? Your Canadian tax to-do list
description: Leaving Canada for India in 2026? Here's what to file with the CRA: your final return, departure tax forms, and what happens to your accounts and benefits.
body_html:
If you moved from Canada to India for good in 2026, Canada still expects one more tax return from you: a "final" return for the part of the year you lived here.

Are you an "emigrant" for tax purposes?

Moving away is not enough on its own. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) treats you as an emigrant when you leave to live in another country and cut your residential ties here. Examples include giving up your Canadian home for a permanent home in India, your spouse or children leaving with you, and closing down your personal and social ties in Canada.

Your date of departure usually falls on the latest of these dates:

  • the day you left Canada,
  • the day your spouse or common-law partner and dependants left, or
  • the day you became a resident of India.

If you kept strong ties (for example, your family stayed in Canada), you may still be a resident of Canada and the rules in this article may not apply. If you are unsure, the CRA's Form NR73, Determination of Residency Status (leaving Canada), lets you ask the CRA for its view.

What to do now: your final Canadian return

For a 2026 move, your final return is the 2026 return. Non-residents file by April 30 of the following year (June 15 if you or your spouse carried on a business), and any balance owing is due by April 30. For a 2026 move, that means April 30, 2027.

  • Use the right package. File using the tax package for the province you lived in on your departure date, for example British Columbia.
  • Enter your departure date on page 1, in the "Residence Information" area.
  • Report world income for the resident part of the year. That means everything you earned anywhere, including in India, from January 1 to your departure date, converted to Canadian dollars.
  • After departure, report only certain Canadian income, such as Canadian employment income. Other Canadian income, such as dividends or pensions, is usually taxed through withholding instead (see below).
  • Credits may be limited for a part-year resident, and moving expenses to India are generally not deductible.

The "departure tax"

When you emigrate, Canada treats you as if you sold most of your property at its fair market value on the day you left, and bought it back right away. Any increase in value becomes a capital gain on your final return, even though you sold nothing. Common examples are shares and mutual funds held outside registered plans.

Some property is not caught by this rule, including:

  • Canadian real estate, such as a condo you keep and rent out,
  • RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, RESPs, RDSPs and pension plans, and
  • for newer Canadians: property you already owned when you arrived (or inherited after), if you lived in Canada for 60 months or less in the 10 years before leaving.

The forms to know:

  • Form T1243 calculates the gains or losses from the deemed sale.
  • Form T1161, List of Properties by an Emigrant of Canada, is required if everything you owned when you left was worth more than $25,000. Cash, bank deposits, registered plans and personal items worth less than $10,000 each are left off the list. It is due by your filing due date, even if you don't otherwise need to file. Filing late can cost $25 a day, up to $2,500.
  • Form T1244 lets you put off paying the departure tax, without interest, until you actually sell. It must be filed by April 30 of the year after you leave. If the federal tax being deferred is more than $16,500, the CRA will ask for security, so contact it before that date.

Your accounts and benefits after you leave

  • Tell your Canadian bank and other payers you are now a non-resident living in India.
  • Withholding tax. Canadian pensions, CPP benefits, RRSP and RRIF withdrawals, dividends and rent paid to non-residents usually have 25% tax withheld, unless the Canada–India tax treaty lowers the rate. Interest from an arm's-length payer is generally exempt.
  • Renting out your Canadian home? You can choose to file a separate return under section 216 to pay tax on your net rental income, which may get you a refund of some withholding.
  • TFSA: you can keep it and it stays tax-free in Canada, but you cannot contribute while a non-resident and you won't get new room.
  • FHSA: you can keep it, but you cannot make a tax-free withdrawal to buy a home while you are a non-resident.
  • Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan balances: special repayment rules apply when you leave, so check these before you file.
  • Benefits stop. Non-residents are generally not eligible for the Canada child benefit or the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026. Tell the CRA your departure date. If payments keep arriving, contact the CRA right away.

A checklist before April 30, 2027

  • Keep proof of your departure date (ticket, home sale or lease end, Indian address).
  • Update your address and residency status with the CRA and your Canadian financial institutions.
  • Get fair market values for your investments as of your departure date.
  • File your 2026 final return, with Forms T1161, T1243 and T1244 if they apply.
  • Remember that India has its own residency and filing rules for your income there.

title: New to Canada in 2026? Your first-year tax and benefits checklist
description: Moved to Canada this year? How to apply for benefits now, file your first return by April 30, 2027, and handle property and income from abroad.
body_html:
Welcome to Canada! If you became a resident in 2026, your first Canadian tax return is due by April 30, 2027. You don't have to wait until then to start: you can apply for family benefits as soon as you arrive. Here is what to do and what to watch for in your first year.

When you become a resident for tax purposes

For tax purposes, what matters is your ties to Canada, not your immigration status. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) looks mainly at whether you have a home, a spouse or common-law partner, and dependants here. For most newcomers, tax residency starts on the first day they live in Canada. The CRA calls that first year your "newcomer year".

If your situation is unclear, for example you still keep a home abroad, Form NR74, Determination of Residency Status (entering Canada), lets you ask the CRA for its view.

What to do now

  • Get a Social Insurance Number (SIN) from Service Canada. It goes on your tax return. If you can't get one, the CRA can give you a temporary tax number.
  • Apply for benefits right away. You don't need to file a return first:
    • No children: Form RC151, to apply for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026.
    • Children under 18: Form RC66, Canada Child Benefit Application, with Form RC66SCH, Status in Canada and Income Information. The CCB application also covers the groceries benefit.
    • Spouse still abroad: Form CTB9 reports their income for the CCB.
  • Report your income from before you arrived. The CRA asks for your world income for up to two years before you became a resident, plus your spouse's. Canada doesn't tax this income, but it uses it to work out your benefits.
  • Write down what your assets were worth when you arrived (see below).

Benefits can be meaningful. The CRA lists the CCB at up to $7,997 a year for each child under 6 and up to $6,748 for each child aged 6 to 17. The groceries benefit is up to $679 a year for a single person. Temporary residents may have to wait until their 19th month in Canada to receive the CCB.

Your first tax return

Your 2026 return is due April 30, 2027. If you or your spouse are self-employed, you have until June 15, 2027 to file, but any tax owing is still due April 30. File even if you earned little or nothing, because the CRA uses your return to calculate your benefits.

  • Enter your date of arrival on page 1, in the "Residence information" area.
  • Income after you arrive: report your world income, meaning money from inside and outside Canada (for example, rent or interest still coming from India), converted to Canadian dollars.
  • Income before you arrive: report only certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done in Canada.
  • Credits are pro-rated. Most credits, including the basic personal amount, are reduced by the share of the year you lived here. The CRA's example: someone resident for 240 days gets about 240/365 of the full amount.
  • Avoid double tax. If income from abroad is taxed in both countries, you may be able to claim a foreign tax credit on Form T2209. Canada has tax treaties with many countries to prevent double taxation.

Property you brought with you

When you become a resident, Canada treats most property you already own, such as shares, mutual funds or valuable collections, as if you bought it at its fair market value on your arrival date. That value becomes your cost for Canadian tax. If you sell later, you are taxed only on growth after you arrived. Keep a statement or valuation showing what each asset was worth on that date. Without it, proving your cost can be hard.

Foreign property reporting (Form T1135)

Canadian residents who own foreign assets costing more than $100,000 in total at any time in a year must file Form T1135. That includes foreign bank accounts, shares of foreign companies and rental property abroad. Personal-use property, such as a holiday home you mainly use yourself, is not included.

The good news: the CRA confirms you don't file Form T1135 for the year you first become a resident. From your second year onward, though, it is due with your return, and the penalties for missing it can be significant.

Savings accounts: RRSP and TFSA

  • TFSA: you start earning room on the day you become a resident, if you are 18 or older. The 2026 limit is $7,000. You don't get room for years before you arrived.
  • RRSP: if 2026 is your first Canadian return, you generally can't deduct RRSP contributions for 2026. Your Canadian earned income in 2026 creates room for later years, and the CRA shows it on your notice of assessment.

Keep records and watch for scams

Keep your notice of assessment and supporting documents for at least six years. You will often need them for mortgages, loans and sponsorship or citizenship applications. The CRA warns that scammers target newcomers. The real CRA will never demand payment by gift card, cryptocurrency or e-transfer, and will never threaten arrest or deportation.

title: Year-end tax checklist: what to do before December 31, 2026
description: Some tax moves only count for 2026 if they happen by December 31. Here's a plain checklist for donations, FHSAs, TFSAs, investment losses and RRSPs.
body_html:
With two months left in the year, now is a good time to check a few tax moves that only count for 2026 if you make them by December 31, 2026. Here is a short, plain checklist for individuals and families in Metro Vancouver.

Why December 31 matters

Several savings and tax-credit rules work on the calendar year, so a step taken on January 2 can land on next year's return instead. The federal government has also scheduled its 2026 budget for November 5, 2026. Budgets can announce new tax measures, so check back after budget day; we'll explain anything that affects this checklist.

What it means for you

Charitable donations

Gifts to a registered charity made by December 31 can be claimed on your 2026 return. A few points worth knowing:

  • You can claim donations from the previous five years that you haven't claimed yet.
  • Spouses and common-law partners can combine their donations on one return.
  • You need an official receipt from a registered charity or other qualified donee. Keep receipts for six years.

Our guide to often-missed tax credits covers this and other credits people forget.

First home savings account (FHSA)

An FHSA lets first-time buyers save for a home with a tax deduction for contributions. Unlike an RRSP, the FHSA has no 60-day window after year end: contributions must be made between January 1 and December 31 to count for that year.

  • Your contribution room starts in the year you open your first FHSA, at $8,000 a year, up to a lifetime total of $40,000.
  • Unused room can carry forward, but only up to $8,000. So opening an account before December 31 starts your room this year, even if you don't put money in yet.
  • You don't have to deduct a contribution in the year you make it. You can save the deduction for a later year when your income is higher.

Tax-free savings account (TFSA)

If you plan to take money out of a TFSA soon, timing matters. Amounts you withdraw are added back to your contribution room only on January 1 of the next year.

  • Withdrawing in December rather than January means you get that room back a full year sooner.
  • Don't put withdrawn money back in the same year unless you are sure you have room. Over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month while the excess stays in the account.

Selling investments at a loss

Some investors sell shares or funds that have dropped in value before year end, to use the loss against capital gains. Watch the superficial loss rule: if you, your spouse or partner, or a corporation either of you controls buys the same investment within 30 days before or after the sale, and still holds it 30 days after, the loss can't be claimed (it is usually added to the cost of the shares bought back instead).

A net capital loss can be carried back three years using Form T1A, or forward with no time limit. Our new capital gains guide explains how gains and losses are taxed.

RRSP

The RRSP dollar limit is $33,810 for 2026 and $35,390 for 2027, according to the CRA. Your own limit depends on your income and past contributions, so it may be lower. Unlike the FHSA, contributions made in the first 60 days of 2027 can still be deducted on your 2026 return, so the RRSP isn't a December 31 deadline for most people.

What to do now

  • Make planned donations by December 31 and keep the receipts.
  • If you're a first-time buyer, consider opening an FHSA before year end.
  • Time any TFSA withdrawals for December if you'll want to re-contribute early next year.
  • Before selling investments at a loss, check what you, your spouse and your company bought in the 30 days around the sale.
  • Watch for the federal budget on November 5, 2026, in case new measures change your plans.

Everyone's situation is different, so check the numbers for your own case before acting.

title: 2027 CPP and EI numbers: lower base CPP rate, higher earnings ceilings
description: CPP's base rate drops to 4.75% each for workers and employers on January 1, 2027, while the CPP and EI earnings ceilings rise. Here's what changes.
body_html:
The numbers that drive 2027 payroll are now mostly in place. The Canada Revenue Agency posted the 2027 Canada Pension Plan (CPP) earnings ceilings on October 28, 2026, and they arrive alongside a cut to the base CPP contribution rate, already passed into law, that takes effect on January 1, 2027. Employment Insurance (EI) figures for 2027 were confirmed in September.

What happened

Three separate announcements now fit together:

  • CPP earnings ceilings are going up. The year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE), the top of the first CPP earnings band, rises to $76,700 in 2027, from $74,600 in 2026. The second ceiling (YAMPE), which caps the "CPP2" band, rises to $87,400, from $85,000.
  • The base CPP rate is going down. Bill C-30, which put the Spring Economic Update 2026 into law, received Royal Assent on June 19, 2026. It lowers the base CPP contribution rate from 9.9% to 9.5% combined, starting in 2027. That is 4.75% each for employees and employers, instead of 4.95%.
  • EI premiums are set. The Canada Employment Insurance Commission confirmed on September 14, 2026 that the 2027 employee rate (outside Quebec) is $1.64 per $100 of insurable earnings, with maximum insurable earnings of $70,800, up from $68,900.

How the new CPP rate works

CPP contributions are made of pieces, which is why the headlines can be confusing:

  • Base CPP is the original plan. This is the part being cut, by 0.2 percentage points for each side.
  • The first enhancement adds 1% on the same band of earnings. Together with the base, employees and employers each pay 5.95% today. The enhancement portion is not part of the cut, so the combined rate on this band falls to 5.75% each in 2027.
  • CPP2 is a separate 4% contribution, each for employees and employers, on earnings between the first and second ceilings. In 2027 that band runs from $76,700 to $87,400.

Before the change, the federal Chief Actuary looked at whether the plan could afford it. The actuarial report published by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions found the 9.5% rate is "sufficient to finance the base CPP over the long term." It also noted that contributions will fall below the plan's expenditures starting in 2027, so the plan will lean more on investment income over time.

What it means for you

For employees, the cut means slightly more take-home pay. Finance Canada estimates a worker earning $70,000 will save about $133 a year in 2027. Higher earners will see some of that offset, because the higher ceilings mean CPP is deducted on a bit more of their pay, and CPP2 applies to a slightly wider band.

Your future CPP pension is not reduced by this change. Benefits are based on your earnings history, not the base rate you paid. If you earn above the new ceilings, you will also build a little more pensionable earnings in 2027.

On the EI side, the higher maximum insurable earnings means the most a worker can pay in 2027 is $1,161.12, up $38.05 from 2026.

What it means for small businesses

Employers match employee CPP contributions, so they get the same saving on base CPP for every employee. For EI, employers pay 1.4 times the employee premium: the 2027 maximum is $1,625.57 per employee, up $53.27.

Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer halves of CPP, so they get the base-rate saving twice, but also pay both halves on the higher ceilings. Owner-managers who take a salary from their own corporation are in a similar position, since the company pays the employer share.

Two practical points for 2027 payroll:

  • Payroll software needs the new rates and ceilings for the first pay date in January 2027. Most providers update automatically, but it is worth checking your first January pay stubs.
  • If you pay yourself through a corporation, the change slightly shifts the math between salary and dividends. It is a good topic for a year-end planning conversation, along with the 2027 RRSP limit, which the CRA lists as $35,390.

What to do now

  • Employees: nothing to file. Expect a small change in your CPP deductions on your first pay in January 2027.
  • Employers: confirm with your payroll provider that the 2027 CPP, CPP2 and EI figures will be loaded before your first January payroll. The CRA had not yet posted its full 2027 CPP maximum contribution table when we checked its pages today.
  • Self-employed and owner-managers: factor the new CPP numbers into your 2027 instalment estimates and your salary-or-dividend decision.

title: CRA's new pre-filled tax return: set up your account by October 31
description: About one million Canadians will be invited to file a pre-filled 2026 return in March 2027. To qualify, your CRA account must be set up by October 31, 2026.
body_html:
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is launching a free service that fills in your tax return for you using information it already has. Starting in March 2027, about one million Canadians will be invited to use it for their 2026 return. To be considered, you need to have your CRA account set up by October 31, 2026.

What is a pre-filled return?

The CRA already receives most of the slips that simple returns need, such as your T4 from your employer or your pension slips. With the new service, the CRA puts that information into a return for you. You sign in, check everything, add anything that's missing, and then accept and submit it.

It isn't automatic filing. Nothing is filed until you review and submit the return yourself, and you stay responsible for making sure it's correct.

Who may be invited

The first round is aimed at people with lower incomes and simple tax situations who don't owe tax. According to the CRA, you must meet all of these conditions:

  • You have a CRA account, and your correspondence preference is set to electronic mail.
  • You filed your 2025 tax return.
  • You were a Canadian resident for tax purposes for all of 2026, you're filing for yourself, and you were 15 or older in 2026.
  • Your income comes only from certain slips, such as T4, T4A, T4A(OAS), T4A(P), T4E, T5 and T5007, and is below a limit that depends on your province, age and disability tax credit status.

You won't qualify if, in 2026, you sold your principal residence, went bankrupt, repaid COVID-19 benefits or amounts under the Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, had exempt income under the Indian Act, or owned specified foreign property costing more than $100,000.

Meeting the conditions doesn't guarantee an invitation. The CRA plans to invite about one million people in 2027 and expand to about 5.5 million by 2029.

What to do by October 31

  1. Sign in to your CRA account, or register if you don't have one.
  2. Check your personal information, including your address and email.
  3. Set your correspondence preference to electronic mail in your account settings.
  4. File your 2025 return if you haven't already. Free options include the CRA's SimpleFile service and community volunteer tax clinics.

If you're invited, you'll get an email in March 2027 telling you the invitation is waiting in your CRA account.

Why filing matters even if you owe nothing

Many benefits are only paid if you file a return every year, including the Canada Child Benefit, the GST/HST credit and several BC credits. A pre-filled return makes it easier for people with simple situations to keep those payments coming.

Is it right for you?

If your only income is from a job or a pension and you have no deductions to claim, a pre-filled return could save you time. But it only includes what the CRA already knows. Credits and deductions that depend on your receipts, such as medical expenses, donations, tuition carry-forwards, moving costs or rent, may be missing unless you add them. If your situation is more than simple, or you're not sure what you can claim, it's worth having your return reviewed.

title: Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%: what it means for you
description: The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate on October 28, 2026, its first increase since 2023, citing higher energy prices and stubborn inflation.
body_html:
On October 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, from 2.25% to 2.5%. It's the Bank's first rate increase since July 2023, and it signals that the long run of rate cuts is over for now.

Why the Bank raised rates

Inflation has been higher and has lasted longer than the Bank expected in the summer. Consumer prices have been rising at around 3% a year since April, and the Bank now expects inflation to reach about 3.5% by the end of 2026. High energy prices are the main driver. When gasoline is left out, inflation was a much lower 2.2% in September.

The Bank's concern is that expensive fuel will spread into other prices, as businesses pass on higher transport and production costs. Raising rates now is meant to stop that from turning into a longer bout of inflation.

The economy has also been stronger than expected. It grew at a 3.3% annual pace in the second quarter, and early estimates suggest about 2% in the third. The Bank expects growth of about 1% for 2026 as a whole, with new US tariffs likely to slow things down in the last few months of the year. Unemployment has been around 6.5% for several months.

What it means for you

  • Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit. Lenders usually move their prime rates in step with the Bank's rate, so borrowing tied to prime generally gets more expensive. Check your lender's notice to see how your payment changes.
  • Fixed-rate mortgages. Your payment won't change until renewal. Fixed rates follow bond yields rather than the Bank's rate directly, and bond yields barely moved on the news.
  • Renewing soon? Compare fixed and variable options carefully, since the Bank has said further increases are possible.
  • Savers. Rates on high-interest savings accounts and GICs may edge up.

What it means for small businesses

Business loans and lines of credit at floating rates will cost a little more. If you carry a balance on a business line of credit, now is a good time to look at your cash flow, pay down expensive debt where you can, and think about how you would handle another increase.

What's next

The Bank said it may need to raise rates further, but will move carefully given the uncertainty around energy prices and trade. Economists at TD expect one more increase in early 2027, which would take the rate to 2.75%. Forecasts like this can change quickly.

The next decision is on December 9, 2026. The Bank's next full economic forecast, the Monetary Policy Report, follows on January 27, 2027.

title: CRA updates for small businesses: online debt payments, Apple Pay and more
description: Business owners can now manage payroll, GST/HST and corporate tax debts online, and pay the CRA with Apple Pay or Google Pay. Here's what's new this fall.
body_html:
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has rolled out several changes this fall that make dealing with it easier for business owners. Here are the ones most likely to matter to small businesses, contractors and corporations.

Manage business tax debts online

Owners, directors and officers can now deal with payroll, GST/HST and corporate (T2) tax balances directly in My Business Account. The new Manage Balance service lets you make a payment, set up a payment arrangement or ask the CRA to call you back, without waiting on the phone. A similar service for personal tax debts launched in October 2025.

One limit to know: accountants and other representatives can't use this service through Represent a Client, so the business owner or a director needs to sign in.

New ways to pay the CRA

Since October 9, 2026, you can pay the CRA with Apple Pay, Google Pay or Konek, as well as by debit card or Interac through participating financial institutions. Whichever way you pay, keep the confirmation with your records.

Keep your director and officer details current

The CRA is reminding corporations to update their records whenever a director or officer joins, leaves or changes their details. Out-of-date information can delay access to My Business Account and stop new representative authorizations from going through.

Rideshare and taxi drivers must register for GST/HST

If you drive for Uber, Lyft or a taxi company, you're generally a self-employed sole proprietor. The CRA's reminder is that rideshare and taxi operators must register for a Business Number and a GST/HST account no matter how much they earn. The usual $30,000 small-supplier threshold doesn't apply to them.

Other changes worth knowing

  • T2 web access code online. Corporations can now get the access code needed to file a T2 return electronically online, without waiting.
  • Faster SR&ED answers. Businesses doing research and development can apply for pre-claim approval, with a decision within eight weeks.
  • Free one-on-one help. The CRA's Liaison Officer Service offers free, confidential visits and sessions for small business owners, self-employed people and landlords.
  • 2027 deadlines. The CRA has published a factsheet of 2027 deadlines for businesses and the self-employed.
  • Extra sign-in security. Individuals and tax preparers can add an optional verification step when filing returns online this coming tax season.

What to do now

  • Make sure you can sign in to My Business Account, and that the right people have access.
  • Check that your directors, officers and addresses are up to date with the CRA.
  • If you owe the CRA and can't pay in full, set up a payment arrangement early. Interest keeps adding up on unpaid balances.
  • Drive for a rideshare platform? Make sure you're registered for GST/HST and charging and remitting it correctly.
